idiom_name: two static buffers + _Atomic(frame *) published with atomic_exchange/store
implementation_notes: The full structure is hand-written: two buffers of the same type, an owner that fills the back one, and exactly one publication step. On C11 and later declare the published pointer `_Atomic(frame *)` and publish with `atomic_store_explicit(&cur, back, memory_order_release)`, reading it with `memory_order_acquire`; a `size_t` index published the same way works when both buffers should live in one array. If a consumer needs a fixed address (a DMA engine writing to a fixed front buffer), copy the finished back buffer over the front under the same synchronization - the pattern survives at O(size) swap cost.
pitfalls: Publishing the pointer before the buffer contents are ordered: without release/acquire (or a critical section) a reader can observe a re-pointed buffer whose writes have not landed yet.
`volatile` is not `<stdatomic.h>`: it does not make an operation atomic and provides no inter-thread ordering - a common embedded misconception.
Readers that keep a `frame_t *` across a swap use the recycled generation; take a fresh load for every pass.
C has no GC: the writer must not reuse a buffer while any reader can still reach it, which requires an explicit handshake when the reader is asynchronous.

variants.name: Interrupt-masked index toggle (no atomics)
variants.idiom_name: volatile index + swap-request flag toggled with interrupts disabled (or a pthread mutex)
variants.implementation_notes: Where atomics are unavailable, or the swap must be atomic against an ISR, keep a `volatile unsigned idx` plus a swap-request flag: the ISR fills the back block and sets the flag, the main loop polls the flag and toggles the index inside a critical section (interrupts masked, or a `pthread_mutex_t` when readers may sleep). This is the classical embedded double buffer; it trades the lock-free property for portability, and the critical section must stay short because masking interrupts adds latency to every interrupt source.
pitfalls: Interrupt masking on the wrong side (or not covering the flag read) still lets the ISR and the loop disagree about which block is current.
A `volatile` index is not atomic on all architectures for wider types; use `sig_atomic_t` or a critical section.
The ISR must never block on a mutex a thread holds; mutex-based swaps need masking or lock-free variants in hard real-time paths.
